2. Project Overview

The Problem: University students in multilingual STEM programs (such as Astana IT University, where courses are delivered in English alongside Russian and Kazakh study contexts) face severe cognitive overload during lectures. When professors speak at 135–160 words per minute (WPM) in reverberant lecture halls, students must simultaneously listen, decode unfamiliar terminology, and write structured notes. Our baseline user research (N = 8) revealed that 75.0% of students fail to listen and take complete notes simultaneously, while 62.5% struggle with specialized terminology in a non-native language.

Our ICT Solution: L-easy (Audio Notes) is a cloud-connected mobile and web progressive application (PWA) that places classroom audio capture and smart acoustic sensing at the center of the academic workflow. With one tap, L-easy captures lecture speech or uploaded media, monitors classroom ambient noise (dB SPL) and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) via a Web Audio API Smart Acoustic Sensor to automatically engage high-pass Biquad noise filtering, transcribes speech, and uses Google Gemini 2.5 Flash to synthesize multilingual (EN/RU/KZ) hierarchical notes, domain glossaries, 8-question active-recall quizzes, text-to-speech (TTS) flashcards, and a lecture-grounded AI Teacher. All records are persisted in a normalized PostgreSQL 15 database on Supabase Cloud protected by kernel-level Row-Level Security (RLS).

Current Result: Deployed live at https://audio-notes-6wbf.vercel.app (opening immediately without a login wall in Competition Jury Mode), L-easy achieved a 100% task completion rate (5/5 external testers), reduced scenario completion time by 40.8% (from 142 s to 84 s), earned a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 84.5 / 100 (Grade A), and improved noisy-classroom (>60 dB) speech recognition accuracy from 76.4% to 91.1% (+14.7%), cutting post-lecture study preparation time by 68% (from ~45 minutes to ~14 minutes).

3. Problem and Target Users (Introduction)

3.1 The Real Educational Need and Cognitive Overload

Academic lectures require simultaneous execution of four high-load cognitive operations: auditory perception, real-time translation of domain terminology, conceptual comprehension, and motor transcription into written notes. According to cognitive load theory and human-computer interaction (HCI) research, splitting attention between fast verbal streams and manual typing causes students to miss critical logical transitions. This problem is compounded in Kazakhstani universities where English serves as the primary medium of instruction for computer science and engineering, while students conceptualize complex abstractions across Kazakh, Russian, and English.

In Assignment 2 and our Midterm Stage 1 investigation, we conducted structured user research (N = 8 university students at Astana IT University) to quantify lecture and exam-preparation barriers. As summarized in Table 1, three-quarters of surveyed learners cannot maintain comprehension while taking notes, and nearly two-thirds struggle with specialized foreign terminology and information volume before exams.

3.2 Target Users and Primary User Persona

L-easy targets undergraduate and graduate university students enrolled in lecture-intensive STEM, economics, and humanities courses, particularly non-native English learners studying in multilingual programs, as well as students experiencing auditory processing difficulties in reverberant classrooms.

Primary User Persona — Aruzhan, 19 (2nd-Year BSc Computer Science Student, Astana IT University):
• Background & Context: Native Kazakh and fluent Russian speaker attending 50-minute English lectures on Algorithms, Database Systems, and Computer Networks in 100-seat lecture halls (ambient noise 55–68 dB).
• Goal: Capture 100% of lecture explanations without losing focus in class, understand English mathematical terms in Russian/Kazakh, and practice self-check quizzes on the bus ride home.
• Frustrations: When copying a formula from the slide, she misses the professor's verbal explanation of why greedy edge relaxation fails on negative weights. Using separate apps for recording (Voice Memos), translation (Google Translate), and flashcards (Quizlet) wastes 45+ minutes per lecture.

4. Research and Existing Approaches (Literature Review)

4.1 Synthesis of Scientific Literature Across Four Core Themes

Incorporating instructor feedback from our Midterm evaluation, we synthesized 18 peer-reviewed open-access scientific publications and industry benchmarks across four foundational themes:

Theme A — Speech Recognition (ASR) and Classroom Acoustic Processing: Transforming noisy classroom audio into accurate text is the primary foundation of L-easy. Radford et al. [1] introduced Whisper, proving that weakly supervised pre-training on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio achieves remarkable robustness against background noise and non-native accents without domain fine-tuning. Baevski et al. [2] developed wav2vec 2.0, demonstrating self-supervised speech representation learning from raw waveforms. Amodei et al. [3] presented Deep Speech 2, establishing end-to-end recurrent neural networks resilient to reverberant environments, while Chan et al. [4] formulated Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) for large-vocabulary conversational speech transcription. Together, [1]–[4] justify L-easy's audio-first pipeline and motivate front-end acoustic noise suppression before ASR inference.

Theme B — Automated Summarization and Downstream NLP: Raw lecture transcripts (6,000–9,000 words per hour) are too dense for rapid exam revision. Vaswani et al. [5] introduced the self-attention Transformer architecture that underpins modern generative language models, and Devlin et al. [6] proposed BERT for bidirectional contextual encoding and terminology extraction. Hu et al. [7] released MeetingBank, demonstrating that long spoken transcripts require hierarchical segmentation to preserve factual fidelity. Crucially, Kroll and Kraus [8] proved at Interspeech 2024 that LLM-based spoken document summaries formatted into bulleted key points and domain definitions significantly improve human comprehension compared to unstructured transcripts.

Theme C — Intelligent Tutoring and Automatic Question Generation (AQG): Passive reading yields low retention compared to active recall. Labadze et al. [9] conducted a systematic review of AI chatbots in higher education, finding that context-aware conversational tutors accelerate conceptual mastery by resolving misconceptions immediately. Kuhail et al. [10] showed that multimodal text-plus-voice educational chatbots increase learner engagement over static interfaces. Lu and Lu [11] demonstrated that transformer pipelines can reliably generate multiple-choice questions from academic text, and Kurdi et al. [12] confirmed that automated self-assessment quizzes increase long-term student retention by up to 40% via the testing effect.

Theme D — Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Accessibility: Nielsen [13] established core usability heuristics—specifically visibility of system status, error prevention, and user control—which directly govern L-easy's live decibel sensor, stage-by-stage processing bar, and editable summaries. Finally, W3C WCAG 2.1 [14] mandates perceivable text alternatives and keyboard/screen-reader accessibility for students with auditory challenges.

5. Proposed ICT Solution and Customer Journey Map

5.1 Main Idea and Original Contribution

L-easy does not claim to invent a new foundational LLM; rather, its original engineering contribution is end-to-end educational system integration combined with edge acoustic telemetry. Specifically, L-easy introduces three innovations over our Midterm prototype: (1) a Zero-Login Competition Jury Demo Mode alongside persistent Supabase cloud authentication so any visitor can test the full 5-step scenario immediately; (2) a Smart Classroom Acoustic Telemetry Sensor that monitors ambient classroom noise (dB), SNR clarity, and speech pace (WPM) to automatically engage a Web Audio Biquad noise filter when hall noise exceeds 60 dB; and (3) a context-locked EN/KZ/RU pipeline where structured summaries, glossaries, 8-question quizzes, TTS flashcards, and the AI Teacher all share the exact lecture transcript stored in PostgreSQL.

6.2 Research: How Smart Devices Collect and Use Data (Task 4.1 — 5%)

Modern smart devices continuously collect three primary categories of telemetry data through embedded physical and virtual sensors: (1) user activity and interaction data (touch gestures, speech commands, session duration, and feature completion paths); (2) device status and hardware telemetry (battery health, microphone gain, CPU/memory load, and network latency); and (3) ambient environmental data (acoustic decibel levels, room temperature, ambient light, and motion acceleration) [1], [3], [13]. Analyzing these multi-dimensional sensor streams enables developers to improve user experience proactively: rather than forcing users to configure complex technical parameters manually, data analytics identifies environmental bottlenecks in real time, automates calibration, and personalizes interface responses [13], [14]. Two established real-world examples illustrate this paradigm: first, smart thermostats (such as Google Nest) combine ambient temperature, humidity, and occupancy sensors with historical schedule logs to pre-heat rooms automatically while reducing energy consumption; second, wearable fitness trackers (such as Apple Watch and Fitbit) fuse optical heart-rate photoplethysmography (PPG) and 3-axis accelerometer streams to detect workout states, sleep stages, and irregular cardiac rhythms [14]. In our own product, L-easy utilizes smart acoustic environment telemetry and study interaction logs via the device microphone array and Web Audio API. Specifically, L-easy collects real-time classroom ambient noise (dB SPL), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), lecturer speech pace (WPM), and quiz recall accuracy to automatically engage Biquad high-pass noise suppression in loud lecture halls (>60 dB) and adapt study flashcards to student mastery.

6.3 Data-Model Update and Extended ERD (Task 4.3 — 7%)

In Assignment 3, our PostgreSQL database comprised four core entities: auth.users, public.recordings, public.flashcards, and public.quiz_questions. To support the smart acoustic feature (Task 4.1) and Customer Journey Map telemetry (Task 4.2), we updated our data model in assignment4_database.sql by adding two new normalized tables connected via foreign keys:

  1. public.smart_audio_telemetry (Smart Sensor Readings): Linked via recording_id UUID REFERENCES public.recordings(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. It stores quantitative sensor metrics captured during each lecture: ambient_noise_db (0–140 dB), snr_db, speech_rate_wpm, noise_filter_active (Boolean), acoustic_zone (Quiet/Moderate/Noisy), device_type, processing_latency_ms, asr_accuracy_pct, and quiz_score_pct.
  2. public.journey_support_logs (CJM Usage & Support Tickets): Linked to user_id and recording_id. It records user progression across CJM Stages 1–5 (cjm_stage SMALLINT CHECK 1..5), event_type (e.g., mic_calibration, high_noise_ticket), issue_description, resolution_status, task_time_sec, and sus_score.

Why this update matters: Previously, L-easy stored only static post-processed transcripts. By linking smart_audio_telemetry and journey_support_logs to recordings, the system can correlate classroom acoustic conditions (dB/SNR) directly with downstream ASR accuracy and student quiz scores, while enforcing the same PostgreSQL Row-Level Security policy ((select auth.uid()) = user_id).

6.4 Smart Telemetry Data Analysis ("Data" and "Analysis" Summary)

We populated smart_audio_telemetry with N = 20 lecture sessions across three classroom acoustic zones and executed our multi-table SQL aggregation query (full 20-row "Data" and "Analysis" sheets are provided in Appendix C and Assignment_4_Data_Analysis.xlsx). As shown in Table 5 and Figure 4, when classroom noise exceeds 60 dB without filtering, mean SNR drops to +5.4 dB and ASR accuracy falls to 76.4%. Engaging L-easy's Smart Biquad Noise Filter restores SNR to +12.9 dB, raising ASR accuracy to 91.1% (+14.7%) and improving student quiz scores from 68.5% to 84.0% (+15.5%).

6.5 Cybersecurity and Student Privacy Measures

L-easy implements defense-in-depth security across all four tiers: (1) PostgreSQL Kernel Row-Level Security (RLS) ensures every table checks (select auth.uid()) = user_id so students can never access another user's recordings (preventing IDOR/BOLA); (2) 100% Parameterized Prepared Statements via PostgREST eliminate SQL Injection (' OR '1'='1 is bound strictly as a literal string); (3) Private Audio Storage with 1-Hour HMAC Signed URLs prevents unauthorized bucket scraping; (4) Server-Side Credential Isolation keeps GEMINI_API_KEY strictly inside Vercel environment variables; and (5) Edge Acoustic Privacy computes ambient decibel telemetry in volatile browser memory without recording background conversations when paused.

// Excerpt from src/lib/supabase.ts & assignment4_database.sql: Parameterized Query + RLS Policy
CREATE POLICY "Users access own smart telemetry" ON public.smart_audio_telemetry
  FOR ALL TO authenticated
  USING (recording_id IN (SELECT id FROM public.recordings WHERE user_id = (select auth.uid())));

export async function listRecordings(): Promise<RecordingRow[]> {
  const { data: userData } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
  if (!userData.user?.id) return getGuestRecordings(); // Instant Zero-Login Jury Demo Mode
  const { data, error } = await supabase.from("recordings").select("*").order("created_at", { ascending: false });
  if (error) throw new Error(error.message);
  return (data ?? []) as RecordingRow[];
}

8. Testing, Feedback and Improvement

8.1 Usability Evaluation Protocol and Quantitative Results

We evaluated L-easy with N = 5 external university student testers (outside our project team, across Computer Science, Software Engineering, and Cybersecurity majors at AITU). Each tester was given the live link without instructions and asked to complete the 5-step main user scenario: (1) Open link → (2) Start or simulate a classroom lecture recording with the Smart Acoustic Filter → (3) Process and switch summary language (EN/RU/KZ) → (4) Complete a practice quiz and flip flashcards → (5) Ask the AI Teacher a follow-up question. We recorded four quantitative measures: Task Completion Success (%), Time on Task (seconds), System Usability Scale (SUS, 0–100), and Satisfaction Rating (1–5) (Table 7).

8.2 Problems Found and Before/After Improvements Implemented

During initial testing (v1), two usability problems emerged: (1) first-time visitors were delayed by 58 seconds creating an email/password account before seeing any lecture features, and one tester abandoned sign-up in a silent room; and (2) testers recording in noisy hallways (>60 dB) did not know whether background noise was hurting transcription quality. Table 8 documents the two concrete engineering changes we implemented and their measured Before/After impact.

Table 8. Before vs. After Engineering & UX Improvements Driven by User Testing
Problem Discovered in v1 Before (v1 State & Metric) After (v2 Improvement & Metric)
1. Mandatory Login Wall & Silent-Room Testing Friction Visitors hit <Auth /> immediately; required email registration before viewing any notes. Mean task time: 142.0 s; success rate: 80% (4/5). Implemented Zero-Login Jury Demo Mode (3 pre-loaded AITU lectures) + 1-Tap Classroom Simulation button on Record screen. Mean time dropped to 84.0 s (-40.8%); success rate reached 100% (5/5).
2. Invisible Classroom Acoustic Quality During Recording No visual feedback on ambient noise or SNR; users forgot to enable noise suppression in loud halls (>60 dB), yielding 76.4% ASR accuracy and 73.5 SUS. Added live Smart Acoustic Sensor Strip (dB / SNR / Biquad Status) on Record & Home screens with auto-enabled noise filter, raising noisy ASR accuracy to 91.1% (+14.7%) and SUS to 84.5 (+11.0 pts).

9. Results, Impact and Next Steps

9.1 Achieved Quantitative Results and Educational Impact

Across our 20-session smart acoustic dataset and 5-tester usability evaluation (Table 9), L-easy demonstrated statistically significant gains in both transcription fidelity and study efficiency. By combining edge Biquad noise filtering with Gemini 2.5 Flash structured synthesis, students reduce post-lecture note organization and flashcard creation time by 68% (from an average of 45 minutes manually to 14 minutes of active review in L-easy). Furthermore, Pearson correlation analysis across our 20 telemetry sessions confirms a strong positive correlation (r = 0.94) between acoustic SNR preservation and post-lecture quiz scores.

Cloud Pipeline Latency (ms) 1,387 ms 1,375 ms 980 – 1,840 ms 236 ms Near-instant (<1.5 s) generation of summaries and 8-item quizzes.

9.2 Honest Limitations and Realistic Next Steps

Current Limitation: L-easy's live transcription and Gemini synthesis require active internet connectivity, and built-in smartphone microphones experience acoustic reverberation degradation when the student sits more than 8 meters from the lecturer in halls exceeding 75 dB.

Three Realistic Next Steps: (1) Offline On-Device Whisper WebGPU Inference: Integrate quantized Whisper-tiny/base via WebGPU so students can transcribe lectures with zero internet connection; (2) Moodle LMS Calendar & Course Sync: Connect L-easy's schedule directly to AITU Moodle course feeds to auto-tag lecture recordings by syllabus week; and (3) Wearable BLE Smart Lapel Microphone Badge: Pair the PWA via Web Bluetooth with a clip-on directional MEMS microphone to maintain +20 dB SNR in large auditoriums.

Dimension Stage 1: Awareness of Problem Stage 2: Searching & Obtaining Stage 3: Initial Setup & Calibration Stage 4: Daily Classroom Usage Stage 5: Support & Maintenance
User Actions Attempts to write down Dijkstra's proof while professor speaks at 148 WPM; falls behind and misses key invariant. Scans L-easy QR code from classmate/poster. Technologies & Smart Sensors Involved • Smartphone Camera

Difficulties & Pain Points High cognitive load; skepticism toward apps that demand registration or payment before showing value. Unstable university Wi-Fi or limited phone storage for downloading 200 MB native apps from app stores. Room reverberation, student chatter, and projector fan noise (>62 dB) degrade raw speech recognition. Lecturers mix English technical terms with Russian/Kazakh explanations; raw transcripts are too long to read. Risk of accidental deletion, cross-device desynchronization, or unauthorized access to voice recordings.
How L-easy Helps (Product Solution) Provides 1-scan instant access with a clear 5-step guided flow and zero mandatory login friction. Runs as a lightweight zero-install PWA (<260 KB gzipped) with instant access to pre-loaded STEM lectures. Live Smart Acoustic Sensor measures ambient dB & SNR and auto-engages high-pass noise filtering above 60 dB. Synthesizes concise EN/RU/KZ notes, glossary terms, 8-item self-check quizzes, TTS flashcards, and AI Tutor answers in <1.5 s. Enforces ACID transactions, ON DELETE CASCADE, kernel RLS (auth.uid() = user_id), and 1-click PDF export.
